doc.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Playing in jazz party settings: space, time and melody
summary: He advises thinking of the band as a group, leaving space, and favoring feeling and melody over streams of notes; Coltrane, Liebman, Miles.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What kind of head do you have to have on to be comfortable in these kind of jazz party situations?

Improvising. Just enjoy the music. I think that’s it. I just enjoy the music. The other thing is, to me, to realize that when you’re playing with a rhythm section, stop thinking of yourself as a soloist and start thinking of the whole band as a group. And that way you don’t have to play every second. See it’s what you don’t play that’s also extremely important I think. In other words if the rhythm section is really grooving, you can play two notes, you can lay out for seven beats, or 14 beats, you can lay out, and then come in with the right note and it’s very effective. If you’re playing — so many players play almost continuous streams of eighth notes. And to me they all wind up sounding basically very much the same. And they do not excite me. There are some special players that play a lot of them, but they’re few and far. In other words, most people just either imitate that play that way, or they play, you know it’s all technique and look how I can run through the changes. There’s so much of that. And people forget about the feeling and they forget

about time, really strong time, and they forget about melodic concept, horizontal concept. There’s a lot of people there that are thinking very vertically. Of course I could be biased, since it’s something I’ve never really taken to. You know since it’s not excited me that much I haven’t gravitated to it and try to learn it in great depth. So again, for educational purposes I’m saying it’s not sour grapes, because I can’t seem to force myself to get into that. It’s not my love. For somebody whose love it is, it’s fantastic. I mean an example of somebody who can do that but does it with great emotion, to me, of course John Coltrane. But somebody around today that does that and does it with great emotion and has it all to me is Dave Liebman. Absolutely incredible harmonic knowledge, can play all over the place, see but David, in addition to playing a lot of notes at one time, he comes out of Trane. And if you listen to a great Trane solo, sometimes you’ll hear Trane playing a million notes but then, after playing all these choruses of a million notes, he might all of a sudden land on one note or one note that has a lot of harmonics in it, or a particular sound he’s getting on it, and what is the most exciting peak of the whole solo? That is. And Miles is an example of somebody who, I mean yeah there’s some records where he plays fast magnificently, but that really wasn’t what it was, it was his sound that gets you. So the right note in the right place is what it’s all about.
Well said. It’s a great concept. One more thought I’d like to ask you —
Feel it. That’s what I mean.
